title: Prime Lamps
statement:
A street has lamps numbered 1, 2, ..., **n**. The mayor decides that exactly the lamps whose numbers are **prime** will be switched on. A prime number is an integer greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ...).

How many lamps will be on?
output: Print one integer: the number of primes between 1 and n inclusive.

samples.explanation: The primes up to 10 are 2, 3, 5 and 7.

hints: Testing every number separately for divisors is too slow for n = 10^7.
Use the Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark all numbers as prime, then for every prime p cross out its multiples p·p, p·p + p, ...
editorial:
Sieve of Eratosthenes: make a boolean array `isPrime[0..n]`, all true except 0 and 1. For p = 2, 3, ... while p·p ≤ n: if p is still marked prime, mark p·p, p·p + p, ... as not prime (smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes). Finally count the true entries. A `vector<bool>` or `bitset` keeps memory small (about 10^7 bits or bytes).

Complexity: O(n log log n).
